data.title: “May I Treasure Up the Words in My Heart!”: Syriac Culture in Modern Aramaic Oral Tradition
data.abstractNote: Modern Aramaic philology is a research field that has attracted the attention of few scholars and vernacular literature preserved in manuscripts appears indeed to be a rather marginal phenomenon in comparison with both oral tradition and Classical Syriac writing (copying of the classical heritage and composition of new original texts). In the last few decades and especially in the last few years, a surprising number of grammatical descriptions of modern Aramaic varieties have appeared. All of them include the transcription and translation of oral texts, some of which are particularly valuable from a literary point of view. Both written and oral texts reveal an extraordinary tenacity of classical stories and motifs. A couple of examples will be given here: the story of the Maccabean martyrs and their mother Shmuni and of Joseph and Mary. In both cases oral transmission has preserved ancient lore in the collective memory of the community, although in rather creative and somehow distorted ways, as is typical of the oral/aural medium.

data.title: Écriture et Écritures dans les poèmes dialogués syriaques
data.abstractNote: Dialogue is confirmed in the most ancient literature for which we have written documentation as a general framework for the structuring of a text, from Sumer to Assiro-Babylonian Mesopotamia and ancient Egypt. Biblical literature has acted as an intermediary for the transmission of Mesopotamian wisdom and for some of its forms of expression in later Jewish and Christian literature. Among some of the late Aramaic literature it is certainly the Syriac Christian literature that has produced and conserved the greater number of discussions and dialogues, in the widest range of poetic forms. The integration of the discussion in hymnography and in liturgical usage explains the vivacity in production and the greater orderliness in the preservation of texts in a Syriac Christian environment. Dialogues in Syriac verse show, moreover, as an excellent example, certain features of Syriac Christianity: 1. The centrality of the Bible and its interpretation; 2. The “Midrashic” aperture to para-biblical accounts, integration and apocryphal detail of biblical accounts; 3. A dense, often inextricable hyper-textual network that connects Syriac, Greek, Hebrew and later Muslim authors; 4. The spreading of exegetic ideas and thoughts through poetry; 5. An extraordinary capacity to adapt, and therefore continuity in time of literary forms; 6. The use of liturgical space as a place for re-processing, transmitting and celebrating shared knowledge.

data.title: La polemica antimanichea nel VI secolo alla luce delle principali fonti di lingua greca: tradizione, interpretazione, innovazione
data.abstractNote: Despite the numerous studies on the Manichaean religion in the Eastern Mediterranean area, there is not yet a comprehensive research or analysis on the main anti-Manichaean works preserved in Greek language from the 6th century, when the religion suffered the last great persecution under Emperor Justinian. This gap in historiography is even more surprising if we consider the important corpus of studies existing on Manichaeism in other centuries, as well as on other religions and so-called Christian heresies during the same period. For all these reasons, my project intends to offer an analysis of the main anti-Manichaean sources from the 6th century preserved in Greek: The Abjuration Formula Capita VII contra Manichaeos, the Disputatio of Paul the Persian against the Manichaean Photeinos, the fictitious Disputatio cum Manichaeo of John the Orthodox, the Homiliae I-II of John the Grammarian, and the account of the Manichaean mythology in Simplicius’ Commentarius in Epicteti Enchiridion. The analysis will be mainly focused on the Manichaean tenets and dogmas conserved in these sources, trying to identify the new knowledge that the Greek literature had of the Religion of Light. In addition, attention will be paid to the influence of other earlier anti-Manichaean works exerted upon these documents to provide evidence about the most characteristic Manichaean dogmas for Greek Christianity. Finally, we wish to develop both a comprehensive compilation and an interrelated analysis of these sources, with the purpose of “filling the gap” in the studies on Greek literature Manichaeism, while offering a useful monograph for further research on Manichaeism in the Eastern Roman Empire during the Late-Antiquity.

data.title: Le Disputationes di Paolo il persiano con Fotino il manicheo: un dibattito fittizio all’epoca di Giustiniano
data.abstractNote: The present contribution examines one of the most interesting anti-Manichaica in Greek literature: the Disputationes of Paul the Persian with a certain master of the Manichaean dogma called Photinus. Among the many doubts surrounding the text, one stands out in particular: its authenticity. The text presents itself as the transcription of a debate held in Constantinople by order of the emperors Justin and Justinian, in the year 527, which would make the Disputationes the only transcription of an authentic debate between Christians and Manichaeans in all preserved Greek literature. This is precisely the stance of the majority of the scholars who engaged with the work: it would correspond to the acts of a dispute that actually occurred. However, the text (which has not been analysed in detail yet) presents too many problems that do not corroborate its authenticity. With this contribution I hope to demonstrate that, conversely to what has been claimed by previous studies, the Disputationes of Paul the Persian appears to be a fictitious work, written at the time of Justinian I. The text reflects the revival of the anti-Manichaean literature of the time, which also coincided with the last great persecution of the Religion of Light in the Eastern Mediterranean, thus marking the extinction from the region (or, at least, a substantial disappearance thereof).

data.abstractNote: "La recherche de ces dernières années sur l'"Evangile de Vérité" s'est très intéressée à la langue et à la structure du nouvel écrit de Nag Hamadi. Certains sont de l'opinion que l'"Evangile de Vérité" est d'origine égyptienne ou copte (Fecht), d'autres, qu'il est d'origine syriaque (Nagel), d'autres, enfin, qu'il est d'origine grecque (Ménard, Böhlig). Il semble beaucoup plus qu'on soit en présence d'un phénomène de bilinguisme, où des expressions ou des tournures grecques sont empruntées à celles du syriaque, plus particulièrement. Mais si l'auteur ou les auteurs ou, encore, le rédacteur final pensaient syriaque, ils n'en écrivaient pas moins en un grec qui demeure hellénistique." (p. 235)

data.abstractNote: ""L'Evangile selon Philippe", est d'origine valentinienne. Il se rapprocherait avant tout du valentinisme des "Extraits de Théodote". En effet, dans l'un et l'autre cas, les images et leur ange se réunissent autour du Christ et de la Sophia, comme les membres autour d'un Tout. Le mythe qui est à la base de ce rassemblement à partir d'une dispersion n'est pas à identifier à celui de l'Osiris égyptien, comme le pensait Reitzenstein, mais à Dionysos Zagreus déchiqueté par les Titans et renaissant lors du regroupement de ses membres. Le nouvel "Evangile" expose une théologie sacramentaire qui est déjà bien en avance sur celle de la Grande Eglise; il l'a même vraisemblablement influencée. Son milieu d'origine, [...] est un milieu syriaque, donc une terre de syncrétisme [...]". (p. 383)

data.title: L’initiation chrétienne selon les Actes de Thomas: l’unité liturgique et théologique du don de l’onction-baptême-eucharistie. Étude historique, liturgique et théologique des cinq “Récits d’initiation chrétienne” selon les versions syriaque et grecque des Actes de Thomas
data.abstractNote: The Acts of Thomas (= AcTh), a corpus handed down mainly in Syriac and in Greek, form part of the apocryphal literature, and narrate the deeds of the apostle Thomas in India. The corpus consists of five Narratives that witness both the actions and the liturgical prayers that help “to become a Christian”. The present thesis is a research from a historical, liturgical and theological point of view on the textual findings of the Narratives based on the two versions that we have today, namely the Syriac version edited by W. Wright and the Greek version edited by M. Bonnet. The first part of the thesis situates the Christian initiation in its historical context and the second part analyses liturgical and theological content of the five Narratives. The third part of the thesis reveals the specificity of the liturgical practice and the theological understanding of the rite of Christian initiation according to the AcTh. The liturgical content being that, at the demand of the candidates for "rušmā" / " sphragis", the apostle gives them “Anointing-Baptism-Eucharist” in a single liturgical celebration. One of the important findings of this research is that the Holy Spirit who is called upon in two of the Epiclesis of the Narratives was not part of the original texts, but is indeed a later addition resulting from the Trinitarian and Pneumatological discussions in the 3rd and 4th centuries. The shift from a Christological perspective, which is present in the entire corpus, to a Pneumatological perspective in the liturgical texts, shows how the AcTh evolved in tune to the theological developments that took place in the history of the ancient Church.

data.title: St. Ephrem’s Understanding of Spiritual Progress: Some Points of Comparison with Origen of Alexandria
data.abstractNote: "The idea of the suhlafe - "transformations" or "changes" of God - a notion addressed briefly by André de Halleux in his essay entitled, "Mar Ephrem Théologien." [...] Here I propose to extend de Halleux's discussion in four respects: First, for Ephrem God's love of human beings leads not only to transformations of Himself at the moments, so to speak, of Creation and Incarnation, but these transformations are both continuous and individualized for each human being. Second, these special concessions of God to humanity have the intention of restoring the "imago Dei" in us both collectively and individually. Third, these notions are quite similar to ideas of spiritual growth found in Origen of Alexandria. Fourth, both Ephrem and Origen use examples drawn from the New Testament to illustrate God's personalized attention to our spiritual life, on occasion using the same exemples to illustrate similar points." (pp. 117-118)
